# 🧭 What Is Quarto? {#what-is-quarto}

[⏱️ 0:05]{.clock}

## Quarto = Markdown → Anything {#quarto-hub}

![](assets/quarto-hub.svg){fig-alt="Two inputs, a .md Markdown file and a .qmd file with code in Python, R, bash, SQL, MATLAB, Java, JavaScript or C, flow into Quarto, shown by its four-quadrant logo, which combines Pandoc with Jupyter and knitr. Quarto produces four groups of formats: documents (html, pdf, docx, odt and, highlighted, epub); presentations (revealjs, pptx, beamer); the web (website, blog, dashboard); and more (Markdown, Jupyter notebooks, JATS, wikis)." width="92%"}

[📚 [All Quarto output formats](https://quarto.org/docs/output-formats/all-formats.html) ·
Quarto logo: Posit, PBC]{.source}

::: {.notes}
Pandoc converts the Markdown. Code cells run in Jupyter (Python) or knitr (R), and their
results are inserted. Quarto's principal languages are Python, R, Julia and Observable
JavaScript (`{ojs}` cells, run in the reader's browser); Jupyter kernels add many more,
such as MATLAB or Java (https://quarto.org/docs/faq/,
https://quarto.org/docs/computations/ojs.html). knitr's engines run `{sql}`, `{c}` and
`{bash}` cells (https://pkg.yihui.org/rmarkdown-book/language-engines.html); in Jupyter,
`!` lines run shell commands
(https://quarto.org/docs/computations/execution-options.html#shell-commands). Today we
use Python only. The official
list groups documents (HTML, PDF, MS Word, OpenDocument, ePub), presentations (Revealjs,
PowerPoint, Beamer), Markdown flavours, wikis and more (Jupyter, JATS, RTF, …):
https://quarto.org/docs/output-formats/all-formats.html. ePub is the e-book format:
https://quarto.org/docs/reference/formats/epub.html. Websites and blogs
(https://quarto.org/docs/websites/) and dashboards (https://quarto.org/docs/dashboards/)
are built from the same files. All checked 2026-10-30. The Quarto logo is a Posit, PBC
trademark, used here to refer to Quarto (https://quarto.org/trademark.html).
:::

In Windows Terminal (the default on current Windows 11) the mouse works as listed: with
text selected, right-click copies it; with nothing selected, right-click pastes. Ctrl+Shift+C
and Ctrl+Shift+V work in every profile, so teach those first for Ubuntu. In PowerShell,
Ctrl+C copies only while text is selected, otherwise it interrupts, and Ctrl+V pastes. The
Edit menu is in the title-bar menu of the older console window, not Windows Terminal, where
the command palette (Ctrl+Shift+P) lists copy and paste actions. Pasting several lines runs
them: read prompts before pressing Enter. Settings differ by version and can be remapped
(https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/terminal/customize-settings/actions). Written from
Microsoft's documentation, checked 2026-11-03 and not yet tried on a Windows machine: try it before teaching. Prompts in this
deck have a copy button, which avoids selecting by hand.

## 📁 Move Around the Terminal {#terminal-basics}

[🏠 before the workshop]{.pace}

::: {.cards .tips}
::: {}
[📍]{.big}

**`pwd`**

where am I?
:::
::: {.fragment}
[👀]{.big}

**`ls`**

what is here?
:::
::: {.fragment}
[🆕]{.big}

**`mkdir name`**

make a folder
:::
::: {.fragment}
[🚪]{.big}

**`cd name`**

go in · `cd ..` goes up
:::
:::

. . .

```text
$ pwd
/home/ana
$ mkdir demo
$ ls
demo
$ cd demo
$ pwd
/home/ana/demo
$ cd ..
```

::: {.check}
💬 After `cd ..`, what would `pwd` print?
:::

::: {.notes}
Everyone, on every system: the rest of the workshop happens in a terminal. The terminal
opens in your home folder, written `~` (here `/home/ana`; on a Mac `/Users/ana`). `pwd`
prints the current folder, `ls` lists it, `mkdir name` creates a folder, `cd name` enters
it, `cd ..` goes up one level and `cd` alone returns home. Lines starting with `$` are what
you type, the others are the answers; do not type the `$`. Tab completes names, and the up
arrow recalls the previous command. Later slides ask you to run
`mkdir -p london-guide && cd london-guide`: this is that (`-p` makes no fuss if the folder
exists). Good answer to the check: `/home/ana`. Try the example in `~/quarto-test` or any
scratch folder, then delete `demo` with `rmdir demo`.
:::

## 🧠 Model + 🔧 Harness = 🤖 Assistant {#model-harness}

::: {.cards .tips}
::: {}
[🧠]{.big}

**Model**

reads and writes text, asks for tools
:::
::: {}
[🔧]{.big}

**Harness**

files, commands, permissions
:::
::: {}
[🤖]{.big}

**Coding assistant**

model + harness in your terminal
:::
:::

. . .

📏 **Bigger, newer model → usually better on hard tasks**

🪶 Small models: fast, cheap, may stumble on multi-step work

✅ **Enough today:** Haiku or Sonnet on **medium** · Sol on **low**

::: {.check}
💬 Which would you pick to fix a typo, and which to join two datasets?
:::

::: {.notes}
The model is the language model (for example Claude, GPT or Gemini). The harness is the
program around it: it gives the model tools to read and write files, run commands and
search, asks you to approve actions, and feeds results back in a loop. Assistants such as the three on the next slide are harnesses; many can run several models, so the same harness behaves
differently with a different model, and the same model behaves differently in a different
harness. Size and quality matter per task: larger, more recent models usually follow
longer instructions, plan multi-step work, and recover from errors better, while small
models are quicker and cheaper and are often enough for short, well-specified edits such as
fixing a typo or reformatting a table. Hard tasks here, such as joining datasets or
debugging a failed render, reward the stronger model. Quality is not only size: training
and recency matter too, and no model is always right, so check its work (the "you
direct and check" rule). Good answer to the check: a small model for the typo, the
strongest available for the join. If a prompt keeps failing, try a stronger model inside
your assistant (see its documentation for how). Model names and availability change
often; do not name versions on stage. For this workshop the prompts are short and
well specified, so Haiku or Sonnet with the effort (reasoning) setting on medium, or
ChatGPT's Sol on low, is sufficient; try a stronger model or higher effort only if a prompt keeps failing.
:::

## 📜 Using AI in Research: Say It, Own It {#ai-policy}

[🏠 before the workshop]{.pace}

::: {.cards .tips}
::: {}
[🚫]{.big}

**Never an author**

AI cannot be accountable
:::
::: {.fragment}
[🔍]{.big}

**You verify everything**

code, numbers, references
:::
::: {.fragment}
[🔒]{.big}

**Keep private data out**

unpublished or sensitive work stays out of public tools
:::
::: {.fragment}
[📝]{.big}

**Disclose the use**

tool + version · task · your checks
:::
:::

. . .

⚖️ Never generate or alter **primary data or images**: that is misconduct

::: {.notes}
Publishers' policies differ, so read the one for your journal, course or employer before
submitting. The common core, from the summary supplied for this deck (not yet checked
against each publisher's own policy page: do that before teaching, and record the date):
AI tools are not listed as authors because they cannot take responsibility; the authors
verify AI output, including facts and references, and answer for plagiarism; unpublished
manuscripts, review reports, participant data and proprietary work are not uploaded to
public AI tools. Where to disclose depends on the use. Basic copyediting (grammar, spelling)
is usually exempt. Drafting or translating text goes in the acknowledgements or a
declaration, with the tool and version. Data analysis and coding go in the Methods, with
enough detail to reproduce them. Explanatory diagrams are disclosed in the caption or
declaration. Generating or altering primary research images or raw data is prohibited.
Publishers also differ in form: some ask for a separate AI declaration with the submission,
some for a note in the cover letter, and some ban AI-generated images outright. This
workshop is a reason to practise: you direct an assistant, so you will have something to
disclose. The next slide shows a statement.
:::

## 📝 Example: An AI Usage Statement {#ai-statement}

[🏠 before the workshop]{.pace}

> During the preparation of this work, the author used Claude Code (Claude Sonnet 5.5) to write
> Quarto files and Python code for the London guide. The author ran all code, checked every
> figure against its source, and takes full responsibility.

. . .

🏷️ **Tool + version** · 🛠️ **What it did** · ✅ **What you checked** · 🙋 **You are accountable**

::: {.check}
💬 Which of these needs a statement: fixing a typo, or computing a table?
:::

::: {.notes}
Adapt it: name your own assistant and model exactly as your assistant names them, with the version, say which tasks
it performed, and keep the last sentence. Put it in the acknowledgements, a declarations
section or the Methods, as the venue asks. Other common forms, from the supplied
summary: for translation, name the tool and say you reviewed the translated sections
so the meaning was preserved; for a diagram made with a generative tool, say which figure,
which tool and version, that you edited and labelled it, and that it fabricates no primary
data; and, optionally, a statement that no AI tools were used. Good answer to the check:
a typo fix is basic copyediting and is usually exempt; computing a table is analysis and
belongs in the Methods, with enough detail to reproduce it, which here is the code and the
`AGENTS.md` that the project keeps.
:::

## 🐧 Let the Assistant Install the Tools {#install-tools}

[🏠 before the workshop]{.pace} 🪟 Windows: in the Ubuntu terminal

::: {.you}
```bash
mkdir -p ~/setup && cd ~/setup && claude    # or: codex, agy
```
:::

::: {.prompt}
```default
Check which of `git`, `curl`, `uv`, `quarto` (1.10 or newer) and the GitHub CLI `gh` are missing on this computer. Install only those, using each tool's official method for my system. Give me any `sudo` command to run myself. Then print every version.
```
:::

🔑 Approve its commands · `sudo` asks for your Ubuntu password (typing shows nothing) · then open a new tab

::: {.notes}
The assistant now does what a block of install commands did before, so the slide holds one
prompt. It must be installed first (previous slide), which is why that slide comes before
this one. An assistant cannot type a `sudo` password, so the prompt asks it to hand those
commands back; the participant pastes them at the Ubuntu prompt, where `sudo` asks for the
Linux password chosen at the first start (typing shows nothing). Behind the prompt the
assistant normally runs `sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y curl git`, uv's installer
(https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/installation/, `~/.local/bin`, so only a new
shell sees it), the Quarto `.deb` from the GitHub release page (Quarto has no Ubuntu apt
package, https://quarto.org/docs/download/) and the GitHub CLI (Ubuntu's own `gh` package
is discouraged, https://github.com/cli/cli/blob/trunk/docs/install_linux.md). On macOS it
uses Homebrew or the same official installers. Needs Quarto 1.10 or later. Behind a
corporate proxy the downloads can fail: tell the organiser before the day. Not yet tried
on a Windows machine with an assistant: run it once in a fresh Ubuntu before teaching.
:::

## ⌨️ Steer the Assistant: /model · /clear · /exit {#slash-commands}

[🏠 before the workshop]{.pace}

::: {.cards .tips}
::: {}
[🧠]{.big}

**`/model`**

bigger model + higher effort = more credits · Haiku or Sonnet on **medium**
:::
::: {.fragment}
[🧹]{.big}

**`/clear`**

task done? **saves credits** · files stay
:::
::: {.fragment}
[👋]{.big}

**`/exit`** · `/quit`

leave the assistant · type `claude` to return
:::
:::

. . .

💸 **Every reply re-reads the whole chat**: a long conversation costs more tokens each turn

🔁 Task done → `/clear` · 🪫 Prompt keeps failing → `/model`, higher effort · ✅ Finished → `/exit`

::: {.check}
💬 One task is finished and an unrelated one starts. Which command first?
:::

::: {.notes}
Slash commands are typed at the assistant's prompt, not in the shell, and they differ a
little between assistants: `/model` opens a picker for the model and, where the assistant
offers it, the effort (reasoning) level. Higher effort thinks longer: slower and dearer, but
better on multi-step work; medium is enough here. Cost follows tokens, and three things
raise them: a bigger model costs more per token, a higher effort writes more thinking tokens
per reply, and a longer conversation is sent back to the model with every new message, so
each later reply costs more than the first (prompt caching makes repeated context cheaper,
not free, and the cache expires). So the habit is: small model, medium effort, one task per
conversation, `/clear` as soon as a task is done. Plans with usage limits or API credits
drain faster with long chats, big models and high effort; many assistants show usage with a
command or status line (type `/` to look). `/clear` drops the conversation so old
instructions and files read earlier stop steering the assistant and stop using up its
context window; nothing on disk changes, and the project's `AGENTS.md` is read again. Use it
between tasks, and when the assistant seems confused. `/exit` ends the session (`/quit` does
the same in assistants that offer it; Ctrl+C twice or Ctrl+D also leave). Starting it again
in the folder begins a new session, and the files persist. Good answer to the check:
`/clear`, because the new task needs none of the old chat. Type `/` alone to list the
commands of your assistant. Command names written from memory and not yet checked against the official lists
(https://code.claude.com/docs/en/slash-commands, https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/codex/cli):
check them in each assistant (`/` lists them) before teaching, since they change often.
:::

## 🛠️ Setup Check {#setup-check}

[🏠 before the workshop]{.pace} 🪟 on Windows, in the Ubuntu (WSL) terminal

::: {.prompt}
```default
Print the versions of `quarto` (1.10 or newer), `uv`, `gh` and this assistant, and run `quarto check`. If `git config --global user.name` or `user.email` is unset, ask me for my name and my GitHub email, then set them. Clone https://github.com/project-delphi/quarto-workshop.git to `~/quarto-workshop` (if it exists, `git pull` only when its working tree is clean) and list its `checkpoints/`. Run `gh auth status`. Run every check even if one fails, then report each as OK or not.
```
:::

::: {.you}
```bash
gh auth login    # only if not "Logged in"
```
:::

🔧 Missing a tool? Rerun the 🐧 install prompt (no assistant? 🧩 install it first) · `gh auth login`: GitHub.com → HTTPS → Yes → web browser, copy the code, open github.com/login/device in Windows · it needs you, not the assistant

### Exercise · ⏱️ 4 min

::: {.done}
`quarto --version` says 1.10 or newer, `uv --version` runs, `gh auth status` says "Logged in", and `~/quarto-workshop/checkpoints/` exists.
:::

::: {.notes}
Quarto 1.10 or newer is needed (current 1.11.x); older ones fail on the London white paper
and the Typst PDF settings. `quarto check` reports Pandoc and Typst. Its Python and Jupyter lines may show "(None)", or
"Jupyter is not available" with an install hint to ignore:
each project gets its own Python environment from uv, by a prompt in each part, so there is
nothing to install for Python now. uv also downloads a Python if the computer has none.
Install uv with `curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh` (on Windows, inside
Ubuntu) or `brew install uv`: https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/installation/
(checked 2026-10-30). Do not debug kernels on stage. A fresh Git has no identity and `git commit`
fails, hence `git config`: use the name and email of your GitHub account (or its
noreply address). The prompt asks for the identity only when `git config user.name` is unset; it makes the assistant ask for them, so the participant types their own, and
you should check the answers are theirs, not placeholders. If `~/quarto-workshop` already exists, the prompt updates it with `git pull`
instead of cloning, so the checkpoints and catch-up steps are current. `gh auth login` stays
a typed command: it is an interactive browser sign-in the assistant cannot complete. Start
the assistant first (`claude`, `codex` or `agy`) in `~/setup`. The cloned workshop
repository supplies the checkpoints and the
water data. `gh auth status` must show a logged-in account before publishing.
PDFs use `format: typst`, bundled with Quarto, so no LaTeX is needed:
https://quarto.org/docs/output-formats/typst.html. GitHub CLI install and `gh auth login`:
https://cli.github.com/ (both checked 2026-10-30).
:::

mkdir -p ~/quarto-test && cd ~/quarto-test
claude    # or: codex, agy

```default
Run `uv init --bare` and `uv add ipykernel nbclient nbformat pyyaml`. Create hello.qmd (html and typst formats): a Python cell computing `6 * 7` and an inline-code sentence showing it. Render it with `uv run quarto render hello.qmd`; check hello.html and hello.pdf both say 42.
```

### Exercise · ⏱️ 5 min

::: {.done}
`hello.html` and `hello.pdf` say 42, and you told the organiser.
:::

::: {.notes}
The setup check proves the tools are installed; this proves they work together, which is
what the first hour needs: the assistant is signed in, can write a file and run commands
you approve, uv builds a project environment, Quarto runs Python through it, and Typst
writes a PDF. It also fills uv's cache, so Part 1's environment step is quicker. Use
`codex` or `agy` instead of `claude` if that is your assistant. Ask participants to confirm
before the day (a reply to the invitation is enough) and follow up with anyone who has not,
or whose run failed: these are the problems that otherwise surface in the tightest block.
Every render prints `[IPKernelApp] WARNING | Kernel is running over TCP without encryption`;
in the dry run of 2026-11-01 (ipykernel 7.4) it came with every successful render and changed
nothing in the output. Tested 2026-10-31 with Quarto 1.6.40 (participants now get 1.11.x; the Quarto 1.10 or newer rule stands, so re-run it once) and uv in an empty folder
(commands run by hand, not
through an assistant). The folder is disposable: delete `~/quarto-test` afterwards. It uses
YAML, a code cell and inline code before their slides on purpose: it is a black-box check
that the tools work together, not a lesson, and the slide says Part 1 explains it.
:::

## 🧰 Three Boxes, Three Roles {#three-boxes}

[👀 An example: you will paste prompts like this from Part 1 on.]{.source}

::: {.prompt}
```default
Create london.md with a level-1 heading "Visit London" and one welcome paragraph.
```
:::

::: {.agent}
writes `london.md` · may run `quarto render london.md`
:::

::: {.you}
approve its commands · open `london.html` in your browser
:::

::: {.notes}
Violet: paste this prompt into your coding assistant (use the copy button).
Amber: what the assistant will probably run; you do not repeat it. Green: the few
things you type or click yourself, such as accounts, publishing and opening files. The
assistant occupies its terminal, so type green commands (such as `quarto preview`) in a
second terminal tab opened in the same folder.
The prompts are examples, not transcripts: assistants vary, so check the result.
:::

## 🧪 Prompts Are Engineered · 🔍 Ask When Unsure {#prompts-engineered}

::: {.cards .tips}
::: {}
[🧪]{.big}

**Engineered prompts**

designed with AI to reduce errors
:::
::: {}
[❓]{.big}

**Don't understand it?**

ask an AI or search the docs
:::
::: {}
[🔍]{.big}

**Dig deeper**

what it does, why, when to use it
:::
:::

. . .

::: {.prompt}
```default
Explain what a Markdown table is and when to use it. Then name the official docs page where I can verify your answer.
```
:::

::: {.notes}
The prompts in this deck were written with AI assistance and refined to reduce the chance
of errors, but they are not magic and assistants vary. Whenever a concept, option or command
is unfamiliar (a YAML key, a Markdown construct, a Python call), do not just paste and move
on: ask your assistant, or read the official documentation, to understand what it does,
why it is used and where else it applies. Understanding the details lets you spot when a
result is wrong and adapt the prompts to your own work. The prompt above is an example of
such a question; use it on any term in the deck.
:::

## 🗣️ How to Prompt Your Coding Assistant {#how-to-prompt}

::: {.cards .tips}
::: {}
[🎯]{.big}

**Be specific**

file names, columns, chart types
:::
::: {}
[☝️]{.big}

**One step at a time**

one task per prompt
:::
::: {}
[✅]{.big}

**Ask it to run & check**

"…render it and tell me about errors"
:::
::: {}
[👀]{.big}

**Check what changed**

you are responsible for the result
:::
:::

🌍 ¿Español? Your first prompt can be: `Responde siempre en español; deja el código y los nombres de archivo en inglés.`

::: {.notes}
A good prompt names the file, the content, the output and a completion check. Browser
translation translates the prompts on the slides, and the copy button copies the
translation; the file names, columns, options and commands in them stay in English, so
the assistant still finds them. You may also write your own prompts in Spanish.
Short follow-ups work once the conversation has context. Ask the assistant to show
what it changed; read the diff before moving on.
:::
